Check out The Crunchbase Megadeals Board . This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here . It was another interesting week for AI-related startup funding, with a number of large rounds and quirky companies. The largest financings went to Tenstorrent , a developer of AI processors and systems, and AI lab Flapping Airplanes . The quirkiest round, meanwhile, was undoubtedly a $200 million financing for Warhound , which wants to breed elite military dogs. A number of big rounds in areas including biotech, space tech and physical AI rounded out the list. 1. Tenstorrent , $1.5B, AI infrastructure: Santa Clara, California-based Tenstorrent, a developer of AI processors and systems, secured $1.5 billion in Series E funding. Trace Capital and Innovation X led the round, which set a $6.2 billion valuation for the 10-year-old company. 2. Flapping Airplanes , $1B, foundational AI: Flapping Airplanes, an AI lab with a focus on developing models that cost less to train and run, closed on $1 billion in Series A funding led by Lux Capital and Index Ventures . The round comes less than 10 months after the year-old San Francisco startup raised a $180 million seed financing. 3. ASI , $325M, AI for critical infrastructure: ASI, a developer of AI technology for securing and operating critical infrastructure in areas such as aviation, transportation and defense, picked up $325 million in Series C financing. Spark Capital led the round, which set a $3 billion valuation for the Boston-based company. 4. Xona , $250M, space tech: Xona, a startup developing a next-generation version of GPS, raised $250 million in Series D funding led by Future Ventures . The round sets a $2.4 billion valuation for the Burlingame, California-based company. 5. Pathos AI , $237M, biotech: Pathos AI, a startup applying AI to drug development, completed a $237 million Series E financing at a post-money valuation around $3 billion. Bristol-Myers Squibb led the financing for the New York-headquartered company. 6. Warp Sciences , $215M, AI, robotics and life sciences: Warp Sciences, a startup applying AI and robotics to help develop new medicines faster, raised a $215M Series A round led by Lightspeed Venture Partners . 7. (tied) Whop , $200M, online business marketplace: Whop, a platform that helps entrepreneurs build and run online businesses, secured $200 million in Series D funding led by Sequoia Capital and Shopify Ventures . The round set a $5.1 billion valuation for the New York-based company. 7. (tied) Star Therapeutics , $200M, biotech: South San Francisco, California-based drug developer Star Therapeutics says it raised $200 million in new financing led by OrbiMed and Janus Henderson Investors . The investment follows Incyte ’s July acquisition of Vega Therapeutics , a subsidiary of Star, in a deal valued at up to $2 billion. 7. (tied) Warhound , $200M, military dogs: Warhound, a startup that wants to breed working dogs for U.S. military forces and emergency responders, launched from stealth with $200 million in seed funding from a long list of backers including Sequoia Capital and 8VC 1 . The startup, co-founded by AnduriI ndustries founder Palmer Luckey , plans to equip the dogs with Anduril technology. 10. Arda Industries , $160M, AI manufacturing software: Arda Industries, a developer of AI-powered software for manufacturing engineering, closed on $160 million in Series A funding at a $1.5 billion valuation, co-led by Altimeter Capital , Accel and Khosla Ventures . The San Francisco-based startup also announced a previously undisclosed $72 million seed financing. Of course, you may believe otherwise if you plan to use your employer’s proprietary information to train an AI agent to do the heavy lifting for you. Seth Kugler, partner at Grellas Shah LLP. That is exactly what the defendant attempted in a recent federal trade secrets case I litigated on behalf of a client in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. In that case, the defendant, a former senior employee at the marketing agency, didn’t just copy client lists to solicit accounts. Instead, he used stolen trade secrets as training inputs to build, essentially, an AI version of his old boss , attempting a shortcut to create a competing business without spending years developing the skills and expertise typically needed to provide such services. AI is creating new ways to misappropriate trade secrets, well beyond the classic theft story of an employee downloading files onto a thumb drive. This case highlights a new reality for founders, exposing unprecedented risks related to AI and trade secrets, employee use of personal devices, and the heightened need for companies to protect themselves in the age of agentic AI. Key lessons for founders AI contamination cannot be undone The defense in this case argued that because their client placed the stolen documents in a “quarantine folder” and no clients had been poached yet, no harm had been done. The court appropriately recognized that the “quarantine folder” was grossly insufficient, granting our temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction while recognizing the competing AI agent as an “existential threat.” An agreement not to touch just the stolen documents themselves is essentially irrelevant once AI gets involved: If a trade secret is used to develop a machine learning model or used to train an AI agent with recursive capabilities, it contaminates the model and the impact can be difficult to undo. Even if raw source files are completely scrubbed of any direct evidence of stolen materials, defendants will struggle to prove to courts that the AI isn’t operating a certain way precisely because it once had access to that proprietary information. Personal devices can pose big risks While trade secret misappropriation has typically been malicious, AI now also creates significant risks of inadvertent violations. Startups frequently scale with employees working on personal devices under standard Confidential Information and Invention Assignment Agreements. Running desktop AI agents on these devices can pose a serious risk.
